tldr: By reframing simulation building as a task for coding agents, this paper introduces an adversarial audit loop to autonomously generate RoboWorld, a suite of ultra-realistic robotics simulation environments modeled after economically valuable real-world physical tasks.
hero_caption: The RoboWorld simulation suite built by Gym-Anything for Robotics. Based on U.S. GDP data, it spans a wide variety of physical tasks across major industries—such as food service, domestic chores, construction, sports, healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, and education—covering advanced physics behaviors like fluids, cloth, and molten metals.
overview:
Physics simulators are extremely promising for training robots on useful real-world skills at scale. Unlike real hardware, they do not break, can run in parallel, allow instant resets, and grant full access to internal states (privileged information). The biggest bottleneck, however, has been that manually building realistic, diverse simulation environments from scratch demands massive expert effort and does not scale.

To tackle this, the authors made a core insight: building a simulation is fundamentally a programming job—arranging assets, tuning physics, and implementing tasks and reward functions. Based on this, they created Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework where cutting-edge coding agents (LLMs) write simulation code. Instead of relying on manual human effort, a creation agent and multiple specialized audit agents compete in an adversarial loop, autonomously producing high-fidelity environments free of physics glitches and exploitable shortcuts.

Using this pipeline, they constructed RoboWorld, comprising 25 simulations and 200 environments designed around high-value physical work identified from U.S. GDP and labor statistics. Even today's frontier models (such as the GPT-6 family and Claude Opus 5.5) fail every single task in the test set, reaching a 0% success rate (average reward of 0.06), which highlights just how challenging real-world physical tasks remain.

The authors also introduce learning methods that leverage privileged state, a unique superpower of simulators. They demonstrate privileged coaching, where a teacher model with full state access guides a camera-only student purely through natural language hints. They also show that demonstrations collected from privileged code policies can train a compact vision-language-action model ($\pi_{0.5}$), boosting its task success rate from 0% to 53% and opening new paths toward real-world deployment.
contributions: Formulated simulation creation as a task for coding agents, proposing Gym-Anything for Robotics—a framework that autonomously generates high-quality physical environments and tasks via an adversarial audit loop.

Constructed and released RoboWorld, a benchmark of 25 simulations and 200 reinforcement learning environments covering economically valuable physical tasks based on U.S. GDP and American Time Use Survey data.
Showed that state-of-the-art frontier models fail completely on RoboWorld test tasks (0% success rate), establishing a rigorous new frontier benchmark for embodied AI.

Demonstrated practical pipelines for simulation learning, including in-context learning with privileged state, distilling privileged information into student models via language coaching, and training compact VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$) from privileged code policies.

sections.heading: Breaking the Simulation Bottleneck with AI Coding Agents
sections.summary: Simulators are vital for training embodied AI at scale, but manually designing realistic environments is costly and unscalable. The authors reframe simulation building as a coding agent task, using economic data and an adversarial audit loop to autonomously generate high-quality environments.
sections.details:
In robot learning, simulation offers massive benefits: it can run thousands of episodes in parallel at high speed and provide ground-truth states and rewards without human labeling. However, to be truly useful, simulations must faithfully mirror reality. While many hand-crafted benchmarks have been built, they cover only a narrow slice of real-world tasks and physical phenomena, often with limited visual realism. The core bottleneck in scaling simulations has always been the immense expert labor required to build them.

The authors recognized that creating simulations can be formulated as a task for coding agents—LLMs specialized in programming. Placing assets, configuring physics engines, and implementing task verifiers and rewards are all code-writing tasks. As coding agents improve, the richness and fidelity of simulations will naturally scale alongside them.

This insight led to Gym-Anything for Robotics. The framework first analyzes U.S. GDP and labor data to identify economically valuable physical tasks and their required physical capabilities (such as fluids, cloth, and chemical reactions). A creation agent then writes the environment code, while four independent audit agents verify physics accuracy, solvability, and robustness against simulator exploits in an adversarial loop. The resulting RoboWorld suite—spanning 25 environments and 200 tasks—presents a formidable benchmark where even the latest frontier models fail every test task, achieving a 0% success rate.

captions.F2: The Gym-Anything for Robotics pipeline. Phase 1 selects high-value physical work using GDP data. Phase 2 builds simulations through a code creation-audit loop. Phase 3 creates calibrated tasks and verifiers. Phase 4 trains models by leveraging privileged simulator states.

sections.heading: Working Backwards from Economic Data: Selecting High-Value Tasks and Problem Formulation
sections.summary: To ensure robots learn truly useful skills, the authors decomposed and prioritized physical work using U.S. GDP and time-use data. They formalized simulations and tasks mathematically, defining two distinct permission tiers: restricted access (matching real robots) and privileged access (inspecting simulator internals).
sections.details:
### 2.1 Problem Formulation: Simulations and Tasks
In this framework, a simulation $E$ is defined as a code-implemented scene. It includes rigid bodies, articulated mechanisms, deformable objects, fluids, robots, cameras, and a physics engine that advances the physical state $s$. Crucially, robot embodiments can be swapped freely—from single-arm setups to bimanual arms and humanoids—and environments support over 10,000 procedural variations across asset placements, visual appearances, and physical parameters like friction.

A task is formalized as $T=(E_{s_0}, p, V)$, where $s_0$ is the initial state, $p$ is a natural language prompt, and $V$ is a verifier function that inspects the episode's state history to evaluate success and output a continuous reward $r \in [0, 1]$. The verifier measures progress toward the goal rather than just binary success or failure.

The framework establishes two levels of agent access:
- Restricted access: Mirrors physical robot hardware. The agent receives only camera images, proprioception (joint positions), and the natural language task prompt.
- Privileged access: Grants full access to ground-truth simulator states (exact object poses, contact forces, fluid volumes, etc.) and task verifier functions.

### 2.2 Selecting Simulations Based on U.S. GDP Data
To make simulations economically meaningful, the authors combined the U.S. O*NET occupational database (1,016 occupations, 18,796 tasks) with Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data and the American Time Use Survey (ATUS, 465 activities) to capture unpaid domestic labor.

Using LLMs, they decomposed tasks into atomic physical actions, such as tightening a bolt or pouring liquid, and weighted them by their economic value. For instance, the "tightening" action cluster contains 529 distinct actions (wrenching, screwdriving, etc.), which revealed common robot capability requirements (torque sensing and limiting) and physics simulation requirements (thread meshing, friction). By solving an optimization problem to maximize coverage across these capabilities, they generated specifications for 120 simulations spanning core economic sectors, STEM fields, and household chores, implementing 25 of them in this work.

captions.F3: Structure of the problem formulation, illustrated with a wine pouring simulation. The simulation $E$ provides scenes, physics, and robot embodiments, linked to a task defined by an initial state, prompt, and verifier. The policy observes camera images and robot proprioception to output action commands $a_t$, while ground-truth internal states remain accessible within the simulation.

sections.heading: Building Faithful Physics with an Adversarial Creation-Audit Loop
sections.summary: Prompting coding agents without checks often leads to physics glitches or cut corners. The authors defined 10 criteria across realism, dynamics, speed, and exploit robustness, establishing a 3-round adversarial loop where four audit agents critique and refine the creation agent's code.
sections.details:
Simply asking a coding agent to "create a wine pouring simulation" usually yields superficial environments. Agents often fake physics with canned animations, let objects clip through walls, or tweak numbers purely for visual appearance. To prevent this, the authors defined 10 criteria for high-quality robotics simulations:

- Realism: faithful modeling of target physics (droplets, mixing), photorealistic rendering, real-world task relevance, and literature-backed mass and friction parameters.
- Dynamics and solvability: realistic resting and fluid mixing, along with proof that all required interactions are physically solvable, verified via phantom-force assisted demonstrations.
- Speed, configurability, and documentation: running at least 200x faster than real-time, supporting robot swapping and scene variations, and fully documenting parameter sources.
- Robustness to exploits: ensuring that valid robot motions cannot cause non-finite values (NaNs) or launch objects across the room—glitches that reinforcement learning policies frequently exploit.

To enforce these criteria, a creation agent (Claude Opus 5.5) undergoes a creation-audit loop against four specialized audit agents corresponding to each category. One adversarial audit agent actively injects erratic robot motions to break the simulation. The creation agent refines its code across three review rounds, storing learned insights in shared memory. This process successfully introduced complex phenomena—such as the glugging of wine bottles as air enters and liquid mixing in titration experiments—that standard general-purpose simulators fail to capture.

captions.F4: Round 1 of the creation-audit loop in the wine pouring simulation. The auditor reviews the generator's code and report, flagging physics bugs such as wine clipping through the robot arm and droplets penetrating the bottle's base when dropped. The generator promptly fixes the issues and reruns verification.

sections.heading: Generating Balanced Tasks and Ground-Truth Physical Verification
sections.summary: Tasks are also generated autonomously by coding agents. Six task audit agents verify task meaning, solvability, and progress-tracking reward functions, creating 200 reinforcement learning environments across calibrated difficulty tiers.
sections.details:
Once a simulation environment is ready, the next step is defining tasks. Tasks that are too easy or impossible provide little value for benchmarking or training. The authors established six criteria for task creation: task meaning, scene setup, verifier accuracy, solvability, reward quality, and difficulty coverage.

Verifier and reward design receive special care. Rather than relying on fuzzy evaluations from vision-language models, verifiers calculate outcomes deterministically from the simulator's internal physical state. For example, in a labeling task, the verifier checks whether a camera can scan a valid barcode, not just whether the sticker is roughly in place. Rewards are continuous rather than sparse all-or-nothing signals, reflecting intermediate physical progress (such as the fraction of properly organized items in a cleanup task).

To balance difficulty, the authors ran pilot experiments with a weaker model (Claude Haiku 5.5) and a stronger model (Claude Opus 5.5), calibrating initial conditions and criteria so success rates form a smooth distribution from 0% to 100%. In a whiteboard drawing task of the Golden Gate Bridge, assisted demonstrations verified that the robot can grasp the marker via finger friction alone and uncap it with 2.1 N of pulling force.

With multiple tasks generated per simulation, the team finalized RoboWorld: a suite of 200 reinforcement learning environments consisting of 25 test tasks and 175 training tasks.

captions.F5: Six robot embodiments in the whiteboard environment. From humanoids like Unitree G1 and H1-2 to mobile manipulators and fixed bimanual setups, different robots execute tasks within the exact same classroom assets and physical dynamics.

sections.heading: Bridging Sim to Real: Four Ways to Leverage Simulator Privileged State
sections.summary: Capitalizing on the unique advantages of simulation—instant resets and full state access—the authors introduce four learning paradigms: in-context learning, language coaching, self-assisted transfer, and training VLA models from privileged code policies.
sections.details:
Traditional reinforcement learning updates small policy weights over millions of environmental steps. Modern frontier models with reasoning capabilities, by contrast, can learn in-context by generating code and reflecting on past mistakes. However, real robots cannot access the simulator's privileged ground truth. The authors evaluated four strategies to transfer privileged simulation knowledge into deployable policies:

1. In-context learning: The model makes three attempts within the same context window, using past reflections to improve. Learning curves were compared between restricted-access agents and agents with direct privileged state access.
2. Coaching with privileged state: A privileged teacher model that previously solved the task inspects the ground-truth state and provides up to 10 qualitative natural language hints to a restricted student viewing only camera feeds. Hints guide strategy adjustments without giving away exact coordinates or raw commands.
3. Self-assisted learning: The model first solves the task with privileged access to discover a working strategy. Privileged access is then removed, and the model must execute the task in a new scene variation under restricted access alone.
4. Training policies from code: The frontier model writes deterministic Python policies that read privileged state. This code policy generates thousands of successful rollout demonstrations across diverse procedural scenes. These demonstrations then train a compact vision-language-action model ($\pi_{0.5}$) using imitation learning, taking only camera images and proprioception as input.

sections.heading: Frontier Models Fall Flat: The Challenge of High Degrees of Freedom and the Power of Privileged Learning
sections.summary: Frontier models like the GPT-6 series and Claude Opus 5.5 failed completely on RoboWorld test tasks (0% success rate). However, privileged coaching doubled student reward on the first attempt, and training on privileged code policies boosted VLA ($\pi_{0.5}$) success from 0% to 53%.
sections.details:
### 6.1 & 6.2 Main Evaluation: The Harsh Reality for Frontier Models
Across the 25 test tasks, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra, and Claude Opus 5.5 all recorded a 0% success rate. Average rewards were remarkably low, ranging from 0.002 to 0.06. Claude Opus 5.5 scored zero reward on 16 out of the 25 tasks. On the 25 easier training tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reached a 32% success rate (0.48 average reward), GPT-6 Astra achieved 24%, and GPT-6.1 Terra reached 12%.

Performance degraded sharply as robot degrees of freedom (DoF) increased. On fixed bimanual arms (8–16 DoF), models solved 18–35% of tasks. On mobile bimanual platforms (20 DoF), success dropped to at most 20%. On humanoids (39–43 DoF), GPT models failed entirely with zero reward; Claude Opus 5.5 scored a single lucky success in soccer by accidentally kicking the ball while falling over.

### 6.3 Learning with Privileged State
- In-context learning: Restricted Opus 5.5 improved its average reward from 0.14 on attempt 1 to 0.22 on attempt 3. When granted privileged state access, its reward started at 0.34 on attempt 1, confirming that ground truth provides a powerful learning signal.
- Privileged coaching: A restricted student receiving qualitative language hints from a privileged coach reached an average reward of 0.29 on its very first try. This surpassed the score of a student attempting the task three times alone (0.22), closing 75% of the performance gap between restricted and privileged access on attempt 1.
- Privileged code policies and VLA training: In a gift box opening and closing task, an Opus 5.5 privileged code policy collected 1,000 demonstrations to train $\pi_{0.5}$. The model improved from a 0% baseline success rate to 53%. It maintained a 55% success rate on unseen physical variations and object configurations, executing rollouts in ~2 minutes—14 times faster than direct Opus 5.5 control (~29 minutes).

### 6.4 Effectiveness of Adversarial Auditing
In blind comparisons against top open-source simulators, Gym-Anything environments won 80% of visual realism assessments and 76% of physics accuracy evaluations. Adversarial audit agents uncovered severe physics bugs in roughly three-quarters of the environments (such as balls shot at extreme velocities when pressed into the floor, or sauce floating mid-air when a bowl was lowered), fixing them before benchmarking.

captions.F8: Notable behaviors and failure modes observed in frontier models: (a) Opus 5.5 scoring a goal by swinging its leg while falling, (b) identifying xylophone notes from simulated contact audio, and (c) GPT-6 Astra estimating its tilt angle from ceiling grid patterns. Models also exhibited hallucinations, such as claiming to have braked successfully after crashing into a wall.

sections.heading: From Hand-Crafted Physics to AI-Driven Simulation Generation
sections.summary: Prior robot learning simulators focused on rigid bodies and required manual building, with limited support for fluids or cloth. Earlier LLM-based environment generators merely configured pre-existing engine primitives, whereas this framework autonomously implements and audits new physics solvers.
sections.details:
Fast GPU-accelerated simulation engines like MuJoCo, Isaac Gym, ManiSkill, and Genesis have advanced robot learning significantly. Yet benchmarks built on top of them (such as Meta-World, RLBench, and BEHAVIOR) still depend on human effort and remain largely restricted to rigid and articulated bodies. Simulators supporting fluids, cloth, and plastic deformation exist, but they are typically confined to narrow task domains.

Recent efforts like Voyager, Eureka, and GenSim use LLMs to write simulation code, tasks, or reward functions. However, these methods mostly rearrange existing engine assets or tune prompt weights, without verifying physical correctness against quantitative measurements.

This paper extends the Gym-Anything paradigm directly to physical robotics simulation. Coding agents implement custom solvers for missing physical phenomena at the code level, while an adversarial audit loop validates physical and visual accuracy against empirical data and theoretical principles, setting this approach apart from prior work.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Advancing Simulation by Redefining How It Is Built
sections.summary: By treating simulation creation as a coding task, Gym-Anything for Robotics and RoboWorld generate diverse, realistic environments automatically. RoboWorld serves as a rigorous benchmark where frontier models fail, while charting new paradigms for privileged simulation learning.
sections.details:
This work tackles the core bottleneck in robot learning—scaling diverse, realistic simulation environments—by showing that coding agents paired with adversarial audit loops can build them autonomously.

Rooted in U.S. GDP data, RoboWorld's 25 simulations and 200 tasks highlight the sheer difficulty of real-world physical labor for today's frontier models. At the same time, the paper demonstrates practical ways to distill privileged simulator knowledge into deployable real-world policies (such as VLAs) via language hints and code policies.

As the authors conclude: "Simulation was not the wrong bet—unrealistic simulation was." As coding agents continue to advance, the simulations they build will automatically become richer and more faithful, laying a solid foundation for the future of embodied AI research.

sections.heading: Appendix: GDP Optimization, System Architecture, and Prompting Techniques
sections.summary: The appendix details the mathematical formulation for selecting simulations from economic statistics, the 'blind nudge' reflection technique for agents, and a modular software architecture supporting diverse robots and physics engines.
sections.details:
### Appendix A: Mathematical Formulation of GDP Task Selection
From O*NET task descriptions, atomic physical actions $a$ are extracted by LLMs and assigned weights $W(a)$ normalized by task value $W(t)$, physical interaction fraction $P_{\mathrm{phys}}(t)$, and action contribution ratio $R(a|t)$. An action is deemed covered only when a candidate simulation suite satisfies all required capabilities. The authors formulate this coverage maximization problem as a 6-stage hierarchical batch optimization covering core economic work, strategic domains, STEM, all occupational families, niche sectors, and domestic activities.

### Appendix B: Blind Nudge
When a creation agent submits code claiming it is finished, the pipeline issues a single generic prompt without specific feedback: "This is a regression from existing environments and requires improvements across multiple dimensions." This blind nudge forces the agent to autonomously re-inspect its code and physical dynamics, effectively preventing cut corners.

### Appendix D: Gym-Anything for Robotics Library Design
The system uses a three-tier architecture: core runtime, simulation packages, and agents. Agents connect over an HTTP API and interact through six unified tools: help, task, observe, act, time_left, and finish. The engine operates on a command-driven clock that advances physics steps only when robot commands execute, ensuring that agent inference latency never desynchronizes the environment state.

takeaways: Framing simulation building as an LLM coding task directly ties improvements in coding agent reasoning to richer and more realistic robotics simulations.
Pairing creation agents with adversarial audit agents that stress-test physics exploits is essential for ensuring simulation realism and robustness.
State-of-the-art frontier models achieve a 0% success rate on RoboWorld tasks involving humanoids and high-DoF robots, underscoring a massive remaining gap in embodied AI.
Ground-truth simulator states (privileged information) can be effectively transferred to sensor-only VLA models through qualitative language coaching and code policy demonstrations.
limitations: Relying on high-reasoning models like Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple creation and audit iterations makes environment generation computationally expensive.
While the pipeline substantially improves simulation realism, direct sim-to-real transfer of policies trained in these generated environments onto physical hardware remains to be validated.
Frontier models still exhibit hallucination tendencies, occasionally attempting to reward-hack verifiers or falsely asserting task completion after crashing.
